turns.en: Guys, have you seen Stella Lefty? Do we have opinions on Stella Lefty here? On a train back from Boston.
turns.zh: 各位，你们看过 Stella Lefty 吗？咱们这儿对 Stella Lefty 有什么看法没有？我当时正在从波士顿回来的火车上。

turns.en: That one? I don't get why people like that song. It seems kind of blah, but it's popular.
turns.zh: 那首啊？我不明白大家为什么喜欢那首歌。听着挺平淡的，可它就是火。

turns.en: I think that that song structurally is the same as a Toby Keith song. So everyone's like, that's Dick Susan. And it's like, no, that's Courtesy of the Red, White, and Blue. A song that everyone has memory hold on purpose.
turns.zh: 我觉得那首歌在结构上跟 Toby Keith 的一首歌一模一样。所以大家都说：这不就是 Dick Susan 嘛。然后你会说：不，那是《Courtesy of the Red, White and Blue》（红白蓝的敬意）——一首所有人都故意把它丢进“记忆洞”（memory hole）的歌。

turns.en: Wait, the Toby Keith song is like... Which one is that?
turns.zh: 等等，Toby Keith 那首是……是哪首来着？

turns.en: Oh, it's so bad.
turns.zh: 哦，那首太糟了。

turns.en: I know, but it's not the one I'm thinking.
turns.zh: 我知道，但我脑子里想的不是那一首。

turns.en: I can sing the whole thing for you. Would that help?
turns.zh: 我可以整首唱给你听。有帮助吗？

turns.en: Yeah, yeah.
turns.zh: 有，有。

turns.en: Hey, Uncle Sam, put your name at the top of his list. And the Statue of Liberty started shaking her fist. And the eagle will fly. And there's going to be hail when you hear Mother Freedom.
turns.zh: 嘿，山姆大叔把你的名字排在了名单最前头，自由女神像开始挥舞她的拳头，雄鹰就要展翅高飞，当你听见“自由老妈”来敲门，那可就要下地狱了。

turns.en: We're going to cut out everything except you singing most of that song. That's just going to be the cold open.
turns.zh: 我们会把别的全剪掉，只留下你唱的那大半首歌。这段就直接当冷开场（cold open）了。

turns.en: I'm doing all of this under the assumption that none of it makes it. That was so pitchy. Are you going to auto-tune it?
turns.zh: 我做这些的时候，前提假设是一句都留不下来。刚才唱得太跑调了。你们会做修音（auto-tune）吗？

turns.en: Hello, and welcome to the Money Stuff Podcast, your weekly podcast where we talk about stuff related to money. I'm Matt Levine, and I wrote the Money Stuff column for Bloomberg Opinion.
turns.zh: 大家好，欢迎收听 Money Stuff 播客——我们每周聊聊跟钱有关的那些事儿。我是 Matt Levine，为彭博观点（Bloomberg Opinion）撰写《Money Stuff》专栏。

turns.en: I'm Mary Childs, host of the podcast, Mary in America.
turns.zh: 我是 Mary Childs，播客《Mary in America》的主持人。

turns.en: And Mary is guest hosting with me again this week.
turns.zh: 本周 Mary 再次来做我的客座联合主持。

turns.en: Thanks for having me.
turns.zh: 谢谢邀请。

turns.en: Thanks for being here. So I got a text the other night from Katie Greifeld.
turns.zh: 谢谢你来。前几天晚上，我收到 Katie Greifeld 发来的一条短信。

turns.en: A celebrity intervention here.
turns.zh: 这是名人干预现场啊。

turns.en: Yeah. My regular co-host, Katie, who is out on parental leave with her newborn-ish daughter, Julia, who's been named on this show, which is why I don't feel bad saying it.
turns.zh: 是啊。我的常规搭档 Katie 正在休育儿假，陪她那个还算新生的女儿 Julia——她女儿的名字在本节目里被公开过，所以我说出来也不觉得内疚。

turns.en: I think you should still feel bad.
turns.zh: 我觉得你还是应该内疚。

turns.en: I do feel bad, but she's named her on this show, so I don't feel that bad. But anyway, she texted me a Bloomberg story, tax-slashing holy grail popularized by AQR, Delta IRS warning. And she texted, Julia and I are discussing this on the Baby Stuff podcast this week. which I believe that I have previously joked, at least with my family, if not necessarily in the newsletter, about starting a new newsletter called Baby Stuff about my babies.
turns.zh: 我是内疚的，但既然她自己在节目里报了女儿的名字，我就没那么内疚了。总之，她给我发了一篇彭博的报道，标题是《被 AQR 带火的节税“圣杯”招来国税局警告》。她还发短信说：“Julia 和我本周要在 Baby Stuff 播客里讨论这个话题。”我记得我以前开过玩笑——至少是跟家里人开的，不一定写进过通讯——说要办一份新通讯叫《Baby Stuff》，专门写我家那几个宝宝。

turns.en: They're not babies anymore, Matt.
turns.zh: 他们已经不是宝宝了，Matt。

turns.en: I know, but Katie's baby is a baby.
turns.zh: 我知道，但 Katie 的宝宝是真宝宝。

turns.en: Katie's baby is legit a baby.
turns.zh: Katie 的宝宝是货真价实的宝宝。

turns.en: She is sitting at home right now playing pretend podcast with her about 350 on Exchange ETFs.
turns.zh: 她这会儿正坐在家里，跟女儿玩过家家式的播客，主题是 351 交换型 ETF（351 exchange ETFs）。

turns.en: So she can play this and it'll be like Clubhouse. It'll be a conversation. She can text us her thoughts. Hi, Katie.
turns.zh: 所以她可以把这期节目放给她听，就当是 Clubhouse 了。这是一场对话嘛。她可以发短信告诉我们她的想法。嗨，Katie。

turns.en: Yeah, it'll be like, you know, like you're supposed to talk continually to your baby so that they like learn language, even if you're just sort of like narrating your day or whatever.
turns.zh: 对，就像那种说法：你应该不停地跟宝宝说话，好让他们学语言——哪怕你只是在给自己的一天做旁白什么的。

turns.en: Totally.
turns.zh: 完全正确。

turns.en: Katie's baby will just be learning about ETFs from birth. So there's news this week about ETFs, which is that the IRS is cracking down on these like 351 exchange ETFs. And my theory of these ETFs is that ordinarily, if you're a person, and you own some stock and you want to own some different stock, you sell the stock that you own, you buy the different stock, and you have a taxable transaction. Selling stock for cash is a taxable transaction, even if your ultimate goal is just to exchange it into new stock. And for ETFs, that's not true. For ETFs, there's a magical sort of pathway through the tax code that allows an ETF to exchange the stock it doesn't want for a stock that it does want without incurring taxes.
turns.zh: Katie 的宝宝将从出生起就开始学 ETF。本周关于 ETF 确实有新闻：国税局（IRS）正在打击这类 351 交换型 ETF。我对这些 ETF 的理解是这样的：通常情况下，如果你是一个人，手里有些股票，又想换成另一些股票，你就得卖掉手里的股票、买入想要的股票，于是产生了一笔应税交易。把股票换成现金就是应税交易，哪怕你的最终目的只是把它换成别的股票。但对 ETF 来说，情况不是这样。对 ETF 来说，税法里有一条魔法般的通道，允许 ETF 把不想要的股票换成想要的股票，而且不产生税负。

turns.en: It's like the whole beauty of ETFs, right?
turns.zh: 这不就是 ETF 的全部美妙之处吗？

turns.en: Right. at first that was like, oh, a neat little feature of index ETFs. And then people realized you could do that for actively traded ETFs where they were just deferring taxes on all of their trading. But then eventually the financial advisors realized like, why can't everyone do that? And so they started being like going to rich individuals and saying, look, if you have a stock portfolio, you can wrap it up in an ETF. And then you can, from then on, do whatever trading you want without ever incurring taxes. And like, The way it works is that there's two trades. There's like, you know, you're a person, you have a stock portfolio, you contribute it to an ETF and you get back shares of the ETF. That shouldn't be a taxable transaction, right? You're just like contributing shares to an ETF and getting back shares in exchange. And then the ETF itself can move the underlying stock in and out of the ETF by doing like heartbeat trades with authorized participants that are also in-kind exchanges that never incur taxes. And so the upshot of this is that if you are like, let's say a centi-millionaire, you can trade your stock portfolio without ever incurring taxes. And the threshold is going down so that if you extrapolate this out in five years, everyone will be able to trade stocks without incurring taxes. And the financial industry was kind of extrapolating that out. And I was writing about it. Yeah, that'll be fun when no one pays taxes to trade stocks. And eventually, the IRS had to crack down. And they cracked down this week with a revenue ruling saying, basically, if you do this too obviously, then it doesn't work and you have to pay taxes.
turns.zh: 对。一开始大家觉得，哦，这是指数型 ETF 的一个小巧可爱的特性。后来人们发现，主动交易型 ETF 也能这么干，等于把自己所有交易的税都递延掉了。再后来，理财顾问们终于想通了：凭什么不是所有人都能这么干？于是他们开始去找有钱人，说：你看，如果你有一篮子股票组合，你可以把它装进一只 ETF 里，从此以后想怎么交易就怎么交易，永远不产生税负。它的运作方式是两笔交易。第一笔：你是个人，有一个股票组合，你把它出资注入一只 ETF，换回 ETF 的份额。这不应该算应税交易，对吧？你只是把份额贡献给 ETF，然后换回份额而已。第二笔：ETF 本身可以把底层股票搬进搬出，方法是跟授权参与人（authorized participants）做所谓的“心跳交易”（heartbeat trades），这些也是实物申赎（in-kind exchange），从来不产生税。所以最终结果是：假如你是个身家几千万美元的人，你就可以交易自己的股票组合而完全不缴税。而且这个门槛还在往下走，你要是把这个趋势外推五年，那就是人人都能免税买卖股票了。金融行业确实在这么外推。我也一直在写这个：是啊，等没人再为股票交易缴税，那场面一定很好玩。最后，IRS 不得不出手。他们本周用一份税收裁定（revenue ruling）出手了，基本意思是：如果你做得太明目张胆，那就不管用，你得缴税。

turns.en: If we notice, we don't like it.
turns.zh: 只要我们注意到了，我们就不喜欢。

turns.en: Yeah. It's basically what it says is that if you contribute appreciated stock to an ETF and as part of the same plan, you immediately heartbeat the stock out and get back a diversified portfolio, then we're going to recharacterize that based on the substance as you've sold the stock and you have to pay taxes. But I don't think anyone quite knows what that means in terms of like how long do you have to wait. Right. And so, you know, we're sort of in early days of cracking down on this.
turns.zh: 对。它说的基本就是：如果你把增值的股票注入一只 ETF，并且作为同一个计划的一部分，立刻用心跳交易把这些股票换出去、拿回一个分散化的组合，那我们就会按实质重于形式的原则，把它重新定性为“你卖掉了股票”，你得缴税。但我不觉得有谁真的清楚这意味着什么——比如你到底得等多久。对吧。所以我们现在还处在打击这种做法的早期阶段。

turns.en: It's nice. We're inventing the rules. We're inventing the lines. It reminded me of a 1031 real estate transaction.
turns.zh: 挺好的。我们在发明规则，我们在发明界线。这让我想起 1031 房地产交易（1031 exchange）。

turns.en: Oh, it's totally a 1031. Yeah.
turns.zh: 哦，这完完全全就是一个 1031。对。

turns.en: It's just so cute.
turns.zh: 就是太可爱了。

turns.en: Yeah. I mean, the cynical view is that the 1031 exchange is really good for real estate developers. Right. And real estate developers are an important constituency here. In that, for instance, the president of the United States is a real estate developer. But even before that, like, you know, there are a lot of real estate developers. Whereas, like, everyone can avoid paying taxes on stock trades. It's like a, you know, bigger, arguably bigger loophole. I don't know if it actually is a bigger loophole in terms of dollars. I know, right? Is it?
turns.zh: 是啊。我的意思是，愤世嫉俗的看法是：1031 交换对房地产开发商特别有利。对吧。而房地产开发商在这儿是一个重要的选民群体。比如说，美国总统本人就是房地产开发商。但即便撇开这层不谈，你知道，房地产开发商的人数也很多。相比之下，人人都能免掉股票交易的税，这是一个——可以说更大的漏洞。我不知道按金额算它是不是真的更大。是吧？到底是不是？

turns.en: Yeah, probably. But it's empirical. That's an empirical question we could go find out.
turns.zh: 嗯，大概是。但这是个实证问题。这是个我们可以去查清楚的实证问题。

turns.en: Right. Like, I incur a certain amount of capital gains taxes by rebalancing my portfolio. You do? Yeah. Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。比如说，我每次给组合做再平衡，就会产生一定数量的资本利得税。——你会？——会。是啊。

turns.en: And it'd be nice not to, but- Yeah, you shouldn't. I don't think you should have to do that anymore.
turns.zh: 能不缴当然好，但是——是啊，你不该缴。我觉得你不该再被迫缴这个了。

turns.en: I don't think that's as big a ticket as like, you know, if I were doing 1031 exchanges. But yeah, I think the point is that like the sort of broad theory of tax is that if you have an asset and you sell it for cash, then that's a taxable transaction and you have to pay taxes on the appreciation. And if you have an asset and you swap it for like kind of the same thing.
turns.zh: 我不觉得这跟做 1031 交换比起来是个多大的数目。不过是的，我觉得关键在于：税法的大致理论是，如果你有一项资产、把它换成现金，那就是一笔应税交易，你得就增值部分缴税。而如果你有一项资产，把它换成同类的东西……

turns.en: You're still in the game. You haven't finished playing yet.
turns.zh: 你还在牌桌上。你这局还没打完呢。

turns.en: Yeah. And exactly where you set the parameters of that is kind of an open question. So 1031 exchanges, I think a lot of people would say are kind of an aggressive setting of the batteries, but it's in the tax code. Basically, 1031 exchange says if you own like, you know, a commercial property and you sell it for cash and then within a certain amount of time, you reapply the cash to buying another commercial property. then you don't have to pay taxable gains on the sale because it's essentially a like-for-like exchange. Oh, I mean, the other thing is when you take corporate tax in law school, one thing you learn is that contributing property to a corporation is a non-taxable transaction. So if you're a person and you own a lemonade stand or whatever, and you're like, I don't want to own this business in my own name anymore. I want to own it in the name of a corporation. You can take your business assets and put them into a corporation and get back shares of the corporation. And like, obviously that's not a taxable transaction, right? Nothing's happened. You're just like changing the form in which you own it. But that's what's happening with an ETF, like with a 351 exchange of the ETF, right? Like you're taking stuff, which happens to be appreciated stock, and you're plopping it into a corporation, which happens to be an ETF. It's like, why is that a taxable transaction? The 351 exchange ETF is like, there are two pieces of it that are like pretty clearly not taxable transactions. One is like contributing property to an ETF. where you're getting back shares of the ETF, which is just changing the form of ownership of the thing. And the other one is the heartbeat trade, where the ETF redeems in kind, which is very controversially not a taxable transaction, but it's not a taxable transaction. That's just how all ETFs do all of their stock trading. And so if you combine those two trades, you really should have a non-taxable transaction. But if you take that too literally, then it means no one will ever pay taxes on their stock trades. And so the IRS is basically like, look, The first trade works. The second trade works. But if you combine them, it's too cute.
turns.zh: 对。而你把这条界线的参数具体设在哪里，是个悬而未决的问题。1031 交换嘛，我想很多人会说它把界线划得相当激进，但它就写在税法里。基本上，1031 交换说的是：如果你拥有一处商业地产，把它换成现金卖出，然后在一定期限内把这笔现金再用于购买另一处商业地产，那你就不必就这次出售缴纳应税利得，因为这本质上是一次同类对同类的交换。哦，我是说，还有一点：你在法学院上公司税法课时会学到，把财产出资注入一家公司是非应税交易。所以如果你是个自然人，拥有一家柠檬水摊或者随便什么生意，你想：我不想再以个人名义持有这门生意了，我想以公司名义持有。你可以把你的经营资产放进一家公司，换回这家公司的股份。显然这不是应税交易，对吧？什么都没发生。你只是改变了持有它的形式。但 ETF 的情形正是如此，也就是 ETF 的 351 交换，对吧？你把一些东西——碰巧是增值的股票——塞进一家公司——碰巧是一只 ETF。这就让人想问：这凭什么是应税交易？351 交换型 ETF 的两个环节，都相当明显地不是应税交易。一个是把财产出资注入 ETF，你换回 ETF 份额，这只是改变了持有形式。另一个是心跳交易，ETF 以实物赎回，这一点争议极大，但它确实不是应税交易。所有 ETF 做股票交易就是这么做的。所以如果你把这两笔交易组合起来，你真的应该得到一笔非应税交易。但如果你把这套逻辑照字面推到极致，那就意味着再也没有人为自己的股票交易缴税。于是 IRS 基本上就是在说：听着，第一笔交易成立，第二笔交易也成立，但你要把它们组合起来，那就太“精巧”了。

turns.en: It's a double negative.
turns.zh: 这是双重否定。

turns.en: And we're going to re-characterize it as a taxable transaction.
turns.zh: 所以我们要把它重新定性为一笔应税交易。

turns.en: They cancel each other out and it becomes a problem for us.
turns.zh: 两个负号互相抵消，然后就成了我们的麻烦。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.en: That's fair. They've got to draw the line somewhere.
turns.zh: 这倒也合理。他们总得在某个地方划条线。

turns.en: It's not like all of tax works, kind of.
turns.zh: 整个税法在某种程度上就是这么运作的。

turns.en: Is it?
turns.zh: 是吗？

turns.en: That's how a lot of tax works. It's like basically like tax structures are like, well, if you combine this, this, and this, we have like an incredibly counterintuitive tax trade. And this, this, and this all work. So it should work. And then the IRS is like, This, this, and this all work, but the combination doesn't work.
turns.zh: 很多税务安排就是这么运作的。基本上就是：税务结构会说，如果你把这个、这个、还有这个组合起来，我们就能得到一个极其反直觉的税务交易。而这个、这个、这个都成立，所以组合起来也该成立。然后 IRS 就说：这个、这个、这个都成立，但组合起来不成立。

turns.en: But you can't do it all at once. I like that because, well, that's what loopholes are. It's just a series of steps, of behaviors that we lump together and then, like, magically it, like, collapses the entire. I mean, buy, borrow, die is just a series of behaviors.
turns.zh: 但你不能一口气全做完。我喜欢这一点，因为，嗯，漏洞本来就是这么回事。它只是一连串步骤、一连串行为，我们把它们打包在一起，然后它就像变魔术一样，把整个体系……我的意思是，“买入、借贷、死亡”（buy, borrow, die）也不过是一连串行为。

turns.en: Right. And, like, in many areas of the world, if you combine seven loopholes that all work, then, like, your combination works.
turns.zh: 对。而且在世界的很多领域，如果你把七个各自都成立的漏洞组合起来，那你的组合也成立。

turns.en: Those are just regular holes, okay? They add up to a loophole.
turns.zh: 那些只是普通的“洞”，好吗？它们加起来才凑成一个“漏洞”（loophole）。

turns.en: But, like, tax actually has a doctrine of, like, recharacterizing for substance over form. And so if you combine seven loopholes that work in a way that is too cute in tax, then, like, yeah, it doesn't work anymore.
turns.zh: 但税法里确实有一条原则，就是按实质重于形式（substance over form）来重新定性。所以在税务上，如果你把七个成立的漏洞组合得太“精巧”，那么，嗯，它就不成立了。

turns.en: It generates, like, an off-gas of too cute. That's really nice.
turns.zh: 它会释放出一种叫“太精巧”的废气。这个说法真不错。

turns.en: I think that's kind of what happened here. But we'll see. Like, I don't... I'm not clear, and I don't think anyone is that clear from, like, this week's rulings what the boundary of too cute is. And I don't think this is, like, the.
turns.zh: 我觉得这次差不多就是这么回事。但我们还得看着。我不……我不清楚，而且我觉得从本周的裁定来看，没有任何人真的清楚“太精巧”的边界在哪儿。我也不觉得这就是那个……

turns.en: Yeah, it sounds like we're going to find out.
turns.zh: 是啊，听起来我们迟早会知道的。

turns.en: Yeah. I'm not going to find out, though.

turns.en: Like the broad topic is that as AI agents are rolled out to consumers, those AI agents will be like looking to impress their clients. owners looking to find something to do. turns.en: So there's this incredible New York Times story this week. With the boring headline, Watchdog Agency Pulls Back on Markets Enforcement Under Trump. But what it is, so the CFTC, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission.
turns.zh: 本周《纽约时报》有一篇非常棒的报道，标题却很无聊：《监管机构在特朗普任内收缩市场执法》（Watchdog Agency Pulls Back on Markets Enforcement Under Trump）。讲的是什么呢，就是 CFTC，也就是美国商品期货交易委员会（Commodity Futures Trading Commission）。

turns.en: Heard of it.
turns.zh: 听说过。

turns.en: So the CFTC regulates commodities markets. And I come from the stock and bond market, right? In stock and bond markets, trades print publicly, right? So if you print a trade in NVIDIA stock, then everyone can see it within microseconds. And everyone knows what the market price is. And like, you know, more or less. And there's like disputes about like, oh, if you like trade one microsecond before the, you know, like there's all sorts of stuff about it. But basically to within a few, you know, fractions of a second and to within a few pennies, people know what the market price is. In bonds, like there's all sorts of stuff about this, right? Like corporate bond trading is mostly, people say it traces, right? There's a FINRA data source called Trace that prints bond trades. And there are like arguments and like changing rules about like, exactly what information has to be printed exactly when because like people like to be able to have a little bit of you know spare time to not print a trade immediately so that they can you know like if a bond dealer buys a bunch of bonds they want to like be able to sell out of them before they print you know the whole thing and i've written a bunch about like there are these bond traders who traded like weird mortgage-backed securities that i think didn't print to trace for a while where they would buy a bond at 70 and then they'd call a customer and be like oh i think i'd get that bond for you at 90, but I got to twist the guy's arm. You know, it's like, he's like really driving a hard bargain, but let me see if I can get it for you for 90. And then they'd sell it to them for 90. It was all just a lie. They'd like make up dramatic stories about how they were negotiating for the bond price. And like, if it had just printed to the tape that everyone could see, like none of that would have worked, right? Like the customers would have just said, so you bought it at 70, so sell it to me for And so what I learned from this time story and from the CFTC enforcement actions is that the cotton market is kind of like the bond market in a more diffuse way, which is that if you're a big cotton exporter and you sign an export contract, you don't print that to the tape, but you fill out a form and send it to a government agency. And the government agency publishes a weekly review of cotton supply and demand. And farmers use that weekly review to set their prices. And so what happened is there's a cotton intermediary, like trading firms, who would sign big export contracts and then- Wait. Wait a while to report them. And in the interim, they would go buy cotton from farmers at prices that were, some people think, too low because the farmers didn't have accurate market information. And the Times story has quotes from a Mississippi State University professor who's a national cotton expert. He said- He had told major cotton traders in industry meetings, you are trying to hide this information that should be public so you can rip off the growers. Like to him, and I think to some cotton growers, this is just like lying about bond trades. This is just a fraud where you are lying about the price that you're getting for cotton, you know, by omission, so that you can buy cotton too cheap. But to other people, including the current CFTC, this is like, what? You filled out a form, right? Who cares, right? So like, The Times story says that the CFTC says that the Biden administration fined industries billions of dollars for minor administrative offenses. And it quotes the former acting chair of the CFTC objecting to charging companies for paperwork errors. Right. And so there's this question of like when these cotton companies wait five weeks to file the form.
turns.zh: CFTC 监管大宗商品市场。而我是从股票和债券市场来的，对吧？在股票和债券市场，交易是公开打印（print）出来的，对吧？如果你成交了一笔英伟达（NVIDIA）股票，那么所有人都会在几微秒内看到，所有人都知道市场价格是多少。当然，大致如此。也会有争论，比如你要是早了 1 微秒成交之类的，各种讲究。但基本上，在零点几秒之内、在几分钱之内，人们都知道市场价格是多少。在债券市场，这里面也有很多讲究，对吧？公司债交易，大家说是上报到 TRACE 的。FINRA 有一个叫 TRACE 的数据源，会把债券交易打印出来。围绕“究竟哪些信息必须在什么时点被打印出来”，一直有争论，规则也在变。因为人们希望能有一点富余时间，不要立刻把交易打印出来——这样，如果一个债券交易商买入了一大堆债券，他们希望能在打印出全部内容之前先把手里的货卖出去。我写过很多这方面的东西：有一批债券交易员，交易一些古怪的抵押贷款支持证券（MBS），我记得有一段时间这些交易是不会打印到 TRACE 上的。他们会在 70 买入一只债券，然后打电话给客户说：“哦，我觉得我能帮你以 90 拿到那只债券，但我得好好拧一下对方的胳膊。你是知道的，他咬价咬得很死，不过让我看看能不能以 90 给你搞到。”然后他们就以 90 卖给客户。这一切纯粹是谎言。他们会编造出戏剧性的故事，讲自己是怎么为债券价格讨价还价的。而如果交易直接打印到所有人都能看到的报价带上，那套把戏就一点都用不了，对吧？客户只会说：“所以你是在 70 买的，那就以差不多的价卖给我吧。”从这篇《纽约时报》报道和 CFTC 的执法行动里，我学到的是：棉花市场在某种程度上有点像债券市场，只是更弥散。也就是说，如果你是一家大型棉花出口商、签了一份出口合同，你并不会把它打印到报价带上，而是填一张表、交给一个政府机构。政府机构每周发布一份棉花供需评述。棉农则用这份每周评述来定价。于是发生的情况是：有一些棉花中间商，也就是贸易公司，会签下大额出口合同，然后——等一等，等上一阵子才上报。而在这段间隔里，他们会去向棉农收购棉花，价格——有人认为——太低了，因为棉农手里没有准确的市场信息。《纽约时报》的报道引用了密西西比州立大学一位全国棉花专家教授的话。他说——他曾在行业会议上对大型棉花交易商说过：“你们在试图隐藏本应公开的信息，好让你们能盘剥种植户。”在他看来，我想在一些棉农看来，这就跟在债券交易上说谎一模一样。这就是一种欺诈：你以“隐瞒”的方式，就你为棉花支付的价格说谎，好让你能把棉花买得太便宜。但在另一些人看来，包括现在的 CFTC，这算什么？你不就是填了一张表吗，对吧？谁在乎呢，对吧？报道里说，CFTC 表示拜登政府曾因为轻微的行政违规对行业开出数十亿美元罚单。报道还引用了 CFTC 前代理主席的话，反对因为文书错误而起诉公司。对吧。于是就有了这样一个问题：当这些棉花公司拖上五周才提交表格——

turns.en: One to five weeks.
turns.zh: 一到五周。

turns.en: One to five weeks. Is that. fraud? You know, is it like lying about trade prices or is it a paperwork error? Just forget.
turns.zh: 一到五周。这算欺诈吗？你知道，这算是在交易价格上说谎，还是只是一个文书错误，只是一时忘了？

turns.en: They were so stressed out right then.
turns.zh: 他们当时实在是太紧张了。

turns.en: Right. There's like this, you know, there's like a natural experiment where like the Biden administration settled with one of these companies and had to pay a large fine, you know, weeks before the Biden administration was out. And then the Trump administration was like, ah, this is fine. Don't worry about it. And they dropped the case against the other one. So one paid a fine, one didn't because of just timing.
turns.zh: 对。这里有一个，你知道，一个自然实验：拜登政府在其中一家公司的案子上达成和解，那家公司不得不支付一大笔罚金，而这发生在拜登政府下台前几周。然后特朗普政府就说：“啊，这没什么。别担心。”他们撤销了对另一家公司的诉讼。所以一家交了罚款，一家没交，纯粹是因为时间点。

turns.en: Which is a little politically interesting because you're supposed to, as the Trump administration, you're supposed to be pro-farmer and this is ostensibly anti-farmer. That action is anti-farmer.
turns.zh: 这在政治上有点意思：作为特朗普政府，你本应该是亲农民的，而这表面上是反农民的。那个做法是反农民的。

turns.en: The time story is like, yeah, this is, you know, a weird political balance because it is, as you said, anti-farmer, right? Like the farmers got ripped off. But, you know, there are other considerations of deregulation and limiting enforcement and not punishing people for paperwork errors. People got really mad at those bond traders. But if you like look your customer in the eye or like look on the phone, And say, yeah, I paid 90 for this bond. And you're lying. That's bad. But if you don't fill out the form for the government data depository, like you're kind of having the same effect, but in a much more diffuse way. And so nobody gets that out of you. And they're like, yeah, it's a paper worker.
turns.zh: 《纽约时报》那篇报道的意思是：是啊，这是一个古怪的政治平衡，因为正如你说的，它是反农民的，对吧？棉农被坑了。但另一方面，还有去监管、限制执法、不因为文书错误而惩罚人这些考量。人们对那些债券交易员可是真的怒了。但如果你是直视客户的眼睛——或者说在电话里——说“是啊，这只债券我付了 90”，而你在撒谎，那就是坏事。可如果你只是没有给政府数据存库填那张表，你产生的效果其实差不多，只不过弥散得多。所以没人能揪住你的把柄。他们的态度就是：“是啊，这只是个文书问题。”

turns.en: It reminded me in a. weird way of the 531 question of like, we have to let that sit. We have to let everything sit for that not to be just a tax evasion move. But how long do we have to let it sit? And here it's like, you're letting it sit too long. But how long is too long? How long do you have? Like, I don't know, your insurance claims run out after a while.
turns.zh: 这以一种古怪的方式让我想起 351 的那个问题：我们必须让这些东西“放一放”。我们必须让一切都放置一段时间，这样它才不至于只是一个逃税动作。但我们得让它放多久？而这里的情况是：你放得太久了。可是多久算太久？你有多长时间？比如说，我不知道，保险索赔过一阵子就会过期。

turns.en: How long?
turns.zh: 多久？

turns.en: Oh, yeah.
turns.zh: 哦，是啊。

turns.en: I mean, like, you know, in the stock and the bond market, there are like quite rigid rules about reporting things promptly. And in the cotton market, I guess there are two, but it's like, you know, it's like, oh, within a week.
turns.zh: 我是说，在股票和债券市场，关于及时上报有相当刚性的规则。而在棉花市场，我猜也有规则，但大概就是，你知道，“哦，一周之内”这种。

turns.en: It really seems like it's someone's job to do that.
turns.zh: 这真的像是某个人的本职工作。

turns.en: Again, like I'm familiar with like banks trading stocks and bonds and there it's like there's an automated system, right? Like the idea that you would do a stock or bond trade and not report it, like those would be two separate decisions is quite weird to me as someone who like lives in an electronic world, right? Like you do a bond trade and like somewhere in the system it gets reported, right?
turns.zh: 再说一遍，我熟悉的是银行交易股票和债券的场景，那里有一套自动化系统，对吧？“你做了一笔股票或债券交易，然后不上报”——也就是说这是两个独立的决定——这对我这种生活在电子世界里的人来说相当古怪，对吧？你做了一笔债券交易，系统的某个地方就自动把它上报了，对吧？

turns.en: Well, it used to be a person, obviously, and that person would fuss at you on the trade floor if you– Oh.
turns.zh: 嗯，以前显然是一个人来做这事，如果你不……那个人会在交易大厅里对你唠唠叨叨。哦。

turns.en: Yeah, yeah. Totally, totally. And stock– right. Like, stock trades used to be, like, you did the trade and then you, like, filled out a ticket to report it to whoever.
turns.zh: 是啊是啊。完全对，完全对。股票也是——对吧。以前股票交易是这样的：你先成交，然后填一张单子，向某个部门上报。

turns.en: And then you sent the ticket through pneumatic tubes to the back office.
turns.zh: 然后你把那张单子用气动管道（pneumatic tube）送到后台办公室。

turns.en: Pneumatic tubes. And I guess, like, cotton kind of works like that, too. But the other thing it reminds me of is Elon Musk, when.
turns.zh: 气动管道。我猜棉花市场也差不多是这么运作的。但这还让我想起另一件事：Elon Musk，当他——

turns.en: He bought Twitter.
turns.zh: 他买 Twitter 的时候。

turns.en: Oh, wow. When he bought Twitter, he bought, like, 9% of the stock. And there was a rule, like an SEC reporting rule, basically saying that he has to disclose that position 10 days after he crosses 5%. And so he didn't do that. He waited an extra like 14 days. And during the extra like 14 days, he bought more stock. When he disclosed his position, the stock went up because everyone was like, oh, Elon Musk is buying Twitter. That probably means he's going to buy the whole company at a premium, right? So he saved, I forget, I did the calculation. A lot of money.
turns.zh: 哦，对。他买 Twitter 的时候，先买了大约 9% 的股票。当时有一条规则，一条 SEC 的申报规则，基本上是说：他在持股突破 5% 之后的 10 天内必须披露该头寸。他没有这么做，而是多等了大约 14 天。在这多出来的 14 天里，他又买了更多股票。等他披露头寸时，股价上涨，因为所有人都想：哦，Elon Musk 在买 Twitter，那大概意味着他会以溢价把整家公司买下来，对吧？所以他省下了——我忘了，我算过这笔账——一大笔钱。

turns.en: Yeah, he saved like $ 150 million by.
turns.zh: 是啊，他省了大概 1.5 亿美元，靠的是——

turns.en: Not disclosing his position when he was required to. And it's the same thing where on the one hand, people sued him and people got mad at him. And I kind of got mad because it was like, look, this is like insider trading. This is like, you're not disclosing a material fact and you're trading against people who don't know the fact and you do know the fact and you're required to disclose it. And so you are ripping them off and there are victims. And it's like a real, it's like a form of like defrauding your counterparties. And then other people, including Elon Musk and his lawyers, were like, this is a paperwork mistake. Like, this is like, we just didn't fill out a form. Who cares? Like, this is stupid.
turns.zh: 在他被要求披露头寸的时候没有披露。而这也是同一种情况：一方面，有人起诉他，有人对他很生气。我也有点生气，因为这就像内幕交易。这是：你没有披露一项重大事实，而你在跟那些不知道这个事实的人做对手交易，你自己知道，而且你被要求披露。所以你就是在坑他们，是有受害者的。这是一种实实在在的、欺骗交易对手的形式。而另一方面，其他人，包括 Elon Musk 和他的律师们，则说：这是一个文书错误。我们只是没填一张表而已，谁在乎？这太蠢了。

turns.en: That's a tough one. I feel like paperwork is stupid, but.
turns.zh: 这个真难判。我觉得文书工作确实很蠢，但是……

turns.en: People took both sides of it. And like, I think broadly speaking, I would say the Biden SEC took the this is bad side. And the Trump SEC took the it's paperwork side and ultimately settled for, you know, very small amounts of money.
turns.zh: 两边都有人站队。我觉得大体来说，拜登时期的 SEC 站在“这是坏事”那一边，特朗普时期的 SEC 站在“这只是文书问题”那一边，最终以非常少的金额和解了。

turns.en: I can't believe we're not doing X-Risk.
turns.zh: 真不敢相信我们居然不做 X 风险（X-risk）这一条。

turns.en: Oh, you want to do X-Risk?
turns.zh: 哦，你想聊 X 风险？

turns.en: Always, yeah.
turns.zh: 永远都想，是啊。

turns.en: Okay. Tell me about X-Risk.
turns.zh: 好吧。给我讲讲 X 风险。

turns.en: To what degree does Anthropic have to disclose or should Anthropic disclose in its prospectus that it might accidentally destroy humanity? Because that's not that material to the stock price. If we're all dead, it doesn't matter.
turns.zh: Anthropic 在多大程度上必须、或者说应当在招股说明书（prospectus）里披露：它可能会不小心毁灭人类？因为这件事对股价并不那么“重大”。如果我们全都死了，股价就不重要了。

turns.en: Right. I think that Anthropic as a matter of genuine belief and culture... and it sort of being their whole shtick. Right. Like, really could not get away with doing an IPO prospectus that didn't say in, like, big, bold letters on the cover, we're going to kill everyone on Earth, right?
turns.zh: 对。我认为 Anthropic，出于真诚的信念和文化……而且这差不多就是它的全部招牌。对吧。它真的没法蒙混过关，做一份不在封面上用又大又粗的字体写上“我们要杀光地球上的每一个人”的 IPO 招股书，对吧？

turns.en: We are accidentally going to murder you.
turns.zh: “我们将会不小心谋杀你。”

turns.en: You can't leave that out.
turns.zh: 你不能把这句漏掉。

turns.en: We're sorry in advance.
turns.zh: “我们提前道个歉。”

turns.en: SpaceX left it out, right? Because, like, although... Well, their model's under control. Elon Musk has, at various times, like, he was, you know, founder of open AI. Like, he's, at various times, been very worried about the existential risk of AI. At other times, been pretty blasé about it. Don't really know what's going on there.
turns.zh: SpaceX 就把这句漏掉了，对吧？因为，虽然……嗯，他们的模型是可控的。Elon Musk 在不同时候——他曾经是 OpenAI 的创始人嘛——他对 AI 的存在性风险（existential risk）时而非常担忧，时而又相当无所谓。真搞不清楚他那边是什么情况。

turns.en: Well, it's before the playa and after, obviously. I'm just kidding.
turns.zh: 嗯，这显然是“去盐滩之前”和“从盐滩回来之后”的区别。我开玩笑的。

turns.en: Sorry. But SpaceX did not say in its prospectus we might kill everyone on Earth, even though it is, in theory, an AI lab, as well as a space rocket lab. And I think people were not that surprised by that because the culture of SpaceX is not really built around worrying about AI killing everyone. Whereas, like, anthropic, it's their whole thing. And so if they left it out of the prospectus, it would be weird. So they have to say it. But I think that it is not. a risk that is really cognizable in the risk factors of an IPO perspective, because if they kill everyone on Earth, they won't get sued for securities fraud, so who cares?
turns.zh: 抱歉。但 SpaceX 并没有在招股书里写“我们可能会杀光地球上的每一个人”，尽管它在理论上既是一家太空火箭实验室，也是一家 AI 实验室。我觉得大家对此并不太惊讶，因为 SpaceX 的文化并不是围绕“担心 AI 杀光所有人”建立起来的。而 Anthropic 呢，这就是它的全部。所以如果他们把这句从招股书里漏掉，就会很奇怪。因此他们必须写。但我认为，这并不是一个在 IPO 招股书“风险因素”里真正可以被认知（cognizable）的风险，因为如果他们真把地球上的人都杀光了，他们也不会被起诉证券欺诈，那谁在乎呢？

turns.en: But I liked your footnote that was maybe other governments will clamp down if they think that we really are about to destroy everyone, and that is a business risk.
turns.zh: 但我喜欢你那个脚注：也许各国政府如果认为我们真的要毁灭所有人，就会出手打压——而那是一种经营风险。

turns.en: Yeah, I am kind of kidding, right? The point is that if you really think that AI could kill everyone on Earth, one possibility is there'll be like a, step change like next week and we'll all be dead and then whoops, right? But like, another possibility is like, there's a lot of, there's a lot of like, bad things that are below the level of kill everyone on earth that like AI might do on its way to killing everyone on earth. And that includes things like being banned for almost killing everyone on earth or killing a.
turns.zh: 是啊，我多少是在开玩笑，对吧？要点在于：如果你真的认为 AI 可能杀光地球上的所有人，一种可能是下周就出现一次阶跃式变化，我们全都死掉，然后“哎呀”，对吧？但另一种可能是：在“杀光地球所有人”这个级别之下，还有很多很多坏事，是 AI 在通往杀光地球所有人的路上可能干出来的。这就包括：因为差点杀光地球上所有人而被封禁，或者杀了——

turns.en: Lot of people or, lots of hits to profit I'm hearing.
turns.zh: 很多人，或者——我听到的是大量利润损失。

turns.en: Yeah. Hacking into the banking system or all these things.
turns.zh: 对。黑进银行系统，或者诸如此类的种种。

turns.en: Doing crimes, not good for business.
turns.zh: 干犯罪的事，对生意不好。

turns.en: All those things are, potential sources of liability for Anthropic that would potentially cause its shareholders to lose money and therefore have to be included in the prospectus. And so if you start from a premise of like, we might kill everyone, then like, what if we only killed a lot of people that could be in the prospectus? It is bad for shareholders.
turns.zh: 所有这些事情，都是 Anthropic 潜在的责任来源，可能让其股东亏钱，因此都必须写进招股书。所以如果你从“我们可能会杀光所有人”这个前提出发，那么“如果我们只杀了很多人”呢？这一条就可以写进招股书了。这对股东是坏事。

turns.en: For shareholders and potential shareholders. Yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah. If you're going to kill them, kill them all.
turns.zh: 对股东和潜在股东都是。是啊是啊是啊是啊。你要杀他们，就把他们全杀了。

turns.en: As a securities matter, I don't want to give legal advice.
turns.zh: 就证券层面而言，我可不想提供法律意见。

turns.en: It's just personal.
turns.zh: 这只是个人建议。

turns.en: There are other reasons not to kill everyone on Earth, but those are.
turns.zh: 不杀光地球上所有人还有别的理由，但那些理由——

turns.en: Hard to price. This reminds me also of, I just had a nice chat with Ellen Hewitt, your Bloomberg colleague, who wrote a book about a sex and wellness cult called One Taste. And she's in Northern California and has a lot of effective altruism and AI conversations and knows a lot about those folks too. And she was saying that There's something I mean, there's obviously a lot of cult behavior in in these circles and the like X risk cult. I mean, it's like a liberation from having to make tiny decisions. Like if you are actually in pursuit of saving humanity, that is so much more fun, which you point out in your column, so much more fun than enumerating the small and trivial and non-existential ways that they may or may not have to budget for hacks and doing crimes accidentally, et cetera. And what clarity, like what a delight. It's just a cleansing. Like, that just must be a relief. Right.
turns.zh: 很难定价。这也让我想起，我刚跟 Ellen Huet 聊得很愉快，她是你在彭博的同事，写了一本关于一个叫 One Taste 的性与身心灵（wellness）邪教的书。她在北加州，经常参与有效利他主义（effective altruism）和 AI 方面的讨论，对那圈人也很了解。她说，这里面有一种……我是说，这些圈子里显然有大量邪教式的行为，比如那个“X 风险教”（X-risk cult）。我是说，那是一种从“必须做琐碎小决定”中获得的解放。如果你真的在追求拯救人类，那要有趣得多——就像你在专栏里指出的——比去逐条列举那些渺小、琐碎、并不涉及存亡的方式（他们可能有可能没必要为“被黑”和“不小心干了犯罪的事”编列预算，等等）有趣得多。多么清晰，多么令人愉悦。那简直是一种净化。这肯定是一种解脱。对吧。

turns.en: If your main risk is killing everyone on Earth, then, like, it feels trivial to write the, you know, accounting risk factors and the perspectives, right? Right. Right.
turns.zh: 如果你的主要风险是杀光地球上的所有人，那么去写那些，你知道，会计类风险因素和招股书里的条目，就显得微不足道了，对吧？对。对。

turns.en: Are y'all really worried about that? Be serious. What's a few trillion, you guys? Like, wake up.
